Genre banner: Nonfiction (with audio symbol)
Story Title: THE HISTORY OF MONEY

Paragraph 1: Thousands of years ago, people didn't use money. Instead, people bartered for things they wanted. Around 6000 BCE, if someone wanted to buy a new goat, he paid for it with grain. But it took time to agree how much things were worth.
Paragraph 2: Then, in 1200 BCE, people started using cowrie shells as money. The shells were easier to carry than goats or bags of grain.
Callout box: BCE stands for Before Common Era. BCE dates count backwards, so something from 6000 BCE is older than something from 1200 BCE. Can you guess what CE stands for?
Illustrations: Two ancient traders bartering grain for a goat; ancient woman trading cowrie shells for folded fabrics

Paragraph 3: After that, around 1000 BCE, the Chinese started using metal money. At first, they used small metal knives and spades. But this money was difficult to carry and to use. Later, probably between 400 and 300 BCE, people started to use round metal money with holes in the middle.
Question: Why do you think they put holes in the coins?

Paragraph 4: However, around 600 BCE, one of the kings of Lydia, which is part of modern-day Turkey, made the first true coins. These coins had pictures of plants and animals on them. Everyone knew how much each coin was worth.
Words in Context box: Find these words in the reading. What do you think they mean? bartered, metal, valuable, credit card, plastic
firstPrintedLine: After that, around 1000 BCE, the Chinese

contains: Paragraph 5: Soon, many countries made their own coins from valuable metals like silver and gold. This made buying and selling easier.
Paragraph 6: The first paper money came from China between 800 and 900 CE. It was easier to carry than metal coins. European countries didn't start to use paper money widely until around 1600 CE.
Timeline callout box: A timeline is an easy way to see events in order.
Timeline entries: 1200 BCE Cowrie shells, 1000 BCE Knives and spades, 600 BCE First coins

Paragraph 7: After that, money didn't change for many centuries. Then, in 1958, there was the first credit card. People didn't have to use paper money or coins. Instead, they could use a small plastic card.
Paragraph 8: Today, in the 21st century, many people use electronic money. Because it's very easy to move around, people often use it to buy things on the internet.
Question: What type of money do you think is going to be next?
Timeline entries: 800-900 CE First paper money, 1958 CE First credit card

Story Title: THE $100 BILL

Dialogue: 'Hey, Paige, what's your phone number?' asked Nina after school. Paige shook her head. 'You know I don't have a cell phone.' 'Oh, Paige! You really should get one!' Jodie laughed hard. Nina laughed too.
Question box: How do you think Paige feels?

Story text: Paige walked through the park on her way home. In her head, she could hear the girls laughing. Then Paige saw something in the leaves.

contains: Story text: On the other side of the park, there was a cell phone store. Paige looked in the window. There was a beautiful black phone. Paige touched the bill in her pocket. She could buy a cell phone now. $95 ... she thought. That's expensive, but ... no more laughing from Jodie and Nina! Paige went into the store. 'Can I help you?' the cashier asked. Paige touched the bill in her pocket again. 'Um, no, thank you,' Paige answered. I should save the money, she thought.
Illustration: Paige looking into cell phone shop window with price tags ($95, $150, $300)
firstPrintedLine: On the other side of the park, there was a cell phone store.

contains: Story text: Paige's dad sat in the kitchen. He looked really tired. 'Hi, honey,' he said, and gave her a hug. 'Dad? I have an idea,' said Paige. 'Let's go out to a restaurant.' 'Oh, Paige, I'd like to, but you know money is tight right now,' he answered. Paige smiled. 'You don't have to pay, Dad!' 'Where did you find that?' he asked. Paige told him about finding the money in the park. 'There's no way to give it back,' her dad said. 'OK. Let's go. I'm hungry!'

contains: Genre banner: Nonfiction (with audio symbol)
Article Title: Clean Cars
Introductory text: Cars are everywhere! We use them to go shopping, go to school, and go on vacation. Cars are useful, but are there good and bad things about cars?
Question box: What are some good and bad things about cars?
Illustration: Modern multi-lane highway packed with colorful cars

Paragraph 1: A lot of cars use gasoline for energy. Gasoline comes from oil in the ground. Gasoline cars are fast, but they are noisy and make the air dirty. Dirty air is bad for animals, plants, and people. It changes our climate, too.
Words in Context box: Find these words in the reading. What do you think they mean? oil, electricity, gasoline, noisy, expensive, energy
firstPrintedLine: A lot of cars use gasoline for energy.

contains: Paragraph 2: Not long ago, most cars were gasoline cars. Now some cars use biofuels. Biofuels come from plants like corn, but these plants need big fields and a lot of water. These cars make the air only a little dirty. Like gasoline cars, they go fast, but they aren't very quiet. They are very noisy.
Illustration: Green biofuel gas pump and corn field
firstPrintedLine: Not long ago, most cars were gasoline cars.

contains: Paragraph 3: Today, there are clean cars that don't use gasoline or biofuel. These cars use electricity, just like a TV or a lamp. They are fast and quiet. They are clean, but they are expensive.
Callout box: Electric cars aren't new. The first car to go 100 km per hour was an electric car in 1899.
Illustration: White electric car plugged into charging station
firstPrintedLine: Today, there are clean cars that don't use gasoline or biofuel.

contains: Paragraph 4: Other cars use air for energy. They are not very expensive. They are quiet and clean, but they are small and slow.
Diagram: Cross-section of compressed air engine labeled 'AIR'
firstPrintedLine: Other cars use air for energy.

contains: Paragraph 5: Solar cars use energy from the sun. Some of them are fast. There are even races! They are not noisy or dirty, but they can be expensive. Not many people have them.
Conclusion line: Clean cars are one way to have a clean world.
Question box: Would you like to have a clean car? Why or why not?
Illustration: Futuristic aerodynamic solar racing car with solar panels on top
firstPrintedLine: Solar cars use energy from the sun.
